item.title: How to Read Your Gas Meter: Every Meter Type With Step-by-Step Instructions
item.description:
Quick Answer

**To read your gas meter**, look at the dials or digital display from **left to right** and record the numbers shown. For dial meters, if a pointer is between two numbers, always record the **lower number** and ignore red test dials.

  • Dial meters: Read **left to right** (opposite of electric meters), record lower number when pointer is between digits
  • Digital/smart meters: Simply read the number displayed on screen—usually in **CCF** (hundred cubic feet) or **therms**

Track your usage to spot [billing errors](/blog/12-how-to-read-your-gas-bill) and potential gas leaks.

item.title: Stormwater Fee on Your Water Bill: What You
item.description:
Quick Answer

A stormwater fee covers the cost of managing rainwater runoff from streets and properties. It is usually a flat monthly charge on your water or utility bill, separate from your water usage charges. You typically cannot reduce it by using less water, but some utilities offer discounts for installing permeable surfaces or rain barrels.

What Is a Stormwater Fee Exactly?

To understand the stormwater fee on water bill, you must first understand the difference between a utility service and a tax. Many municipalities explicitly state that this charge is a user fee, not a tax. For example, the City of Alexandria, Virginia, clarifies on its official website that the Stormwater Utility Fee is included as a separate line item on the real estate tax bill but is "not a tax." It is a utility user fee modeled after how residents are billed for other services like water and sewer.

item.title: Time-of-Use Electricity Rates: When Power Is Cheapest and How to Save
item.description:
Quick Answer

Time-of-Use (TOU) rates charge different prices by time of day — typically $0.12–$0.15/kWh off-peak vs. $0.25–$0.40/kWh on-peak (usually 4–9 PM weekdays). Shifting laundry, EV charging, dishwashing, and pool pumps to overnight or weekend off-peak windows can cut your electric bill 15–25%.

  • Off-peak hours (nights, early mornings, weekends) carry the lowest rates
  • On-peak hours (typically 4–9 PM weekdays) cost 2–3× more
  • Shift 50% of usage to off-peak to save roughly $30–$60/month

If your utility has offered you a time-of-use rate plan, whether it saves money depends on when you use power. Households that can move most of their usage to off-peak windows save 15–25% on the same kWh; households that can’t shift much often pay more. Your peak-to-off-peak price ratio, how much load you can move, and your current usage pattern are the three numbers that decide it.

item.title: How Do Smart Meters Work? (And Should You Trust Them?)
item.description:
Quick Answer

A smart meter is a digital electricity meter that records your usage in short intervals (usually 15–60 minutes) and sends that data automatically to your utility. Unlike old analog meters with spinning dials, smart meters:

  • Track exactly when you use power, not just how much
  • Report remotely — no meter reader visits your property
  • Enable time-of-use rates — different prices at different hours
  • Eliminate estimated bills — the utility gets actual usage data

Are they accurate? Yes — smart meters are generally more accurate than aging analog meters, which tend to slow down and under-report usage over time. If your bill jumped after a smart meter installation, it is likely because the new meter is catching usage the old one missed. For help diagnosing a sudden increase, see our guide on sudden electricity bill spikes.

item.title: How to Read an Electric Meter (Dial & Digital Guide)
item.description:
Quick Answer

Reading your electric meter: Digital meters show a 5-digit number (ignore any zeros at the right) - subtract last month’s reading from current reading and multiply by your rate (e.g., 12,500 - 10,000 = 2,500 kWh × $0.12 = $300 usage).

  • Fact: Analog meters with 4-5 dials are read right-to-left, recording the number the pointer just passed
  • Action: Check your meter weekly to catch unusual usage spikes before they become expensive problems

For more detail, see Understanding Your Utility Bill.
